```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)

# Fixed seed for the permutation test and for reproducible table ids.
set.seed(2026)

# When the solutions vignette renders this file as a child, `params` is set by
# the parent. The default is the question-only version.
show_solutions <- isTRUE(params$show_solutions)
solutions_only <- isTRUE(params$solutions_only)

# The solution blocks are marked with HTML comments in the document body. The
# document hook below either drops them (question-only version) or drops
# everything except them (solutions-only version).
knitr::knit_hooks$set(document = function(x) {
  lines <- unlist(strsplit(x, "\n", fixed = TRUE))

  # This hook runs once on the child (via knit_child) and once more on the
  # parent document. On the second run the markers have already been removed,
  # so return the already-filtered document unchanged.
  if (
    solutions_only &&
      !any(grepl("<!-- SOLUTION START -->", lines, fixed = TRUE))
  ) {
    return(paste(lines, collapse = "\n"))
  }

  if (solutions_only) {
    # Keep only the solution blocks, and promote their "**Solution N.**"
    # headers to real headings so they appear in the table of contents.
    keep <- rep(FALSE, length(lines))
    inside <- FALSE
    for (i in seq_along(lines)) {
      if (identical(lines[i], "<!-- SOLUTION START -->")) {
        inside <- TRUE
        next
      }
      if (identical(lines[i], "<!-- SOLUTION END -->")) {
        inside <- FALSE
        next
      }
      if (inside) {
        lines[i] <- sub(
          "^\\*\\*Solution ([0-9].*?)\\.\\*\\*$",
          "## Solution \\1",
          lines[i]
        )
        keep[i] <- TRUE
      }
    }
  } else if (!show_solutions) {
    # Question-only version: drop the solution blocks.
    keep <- rep(TRUE, length(lines))
    inside <- FALSE
    for (i in seq_along(lines)) {
      if (identical(lines[i], "<!-- SOLUTION START -->")) {
        inside <- TRUE
        keep[i] <- FALSE
        next
      }
      if (identical(lines[i], "<!-- SOLUTION END -->")) {
        inside <- FALSE
        keep[i] <- FALSE
        next
      }
      if (inside) keep[i] <- FALSE
    }
  } else {
    # Questions and solutions together.
    keep <- rep(TRUE, length(lines))
  }

  paste(lines[keep], collapse = "\n")
})
```

::: {.callout-note}
**About this computer exercise.**

This exercise covers **Chapters 1 and 2** of Collett, *Modelling Survival
Data in Medical Research* (4th ed.). It follows on from the two lectures:
**Lecture 1** (basic principles, censoring and the Kaplan–Meier estimator) and
**Lecture 2** (the hazard and cumulative hazard, the Nelson–Aalen estimator and
the log-rank test). Where a question builds on a lecture slide, the slide is
noted next to the question.

:::

## Data and software

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(sta310r)
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)
library(gtsummary)
library(broom)
```

```{r solutions-support, include = FALSE}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
}

fmt_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
}

pct <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = digits), " %")
}

surv_at <- function(fit, times) {
  s <- summary(fit, times = times, extend = TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(
    time = s$time,
    n.risk = s$n.risk,
    S = s$surv,
    se = s$std.err,
    lower = s$lower,
    upper = s$upper
  )
}

km_iud <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = iud)

km_myeloma <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = sta310r::myeloma)
km_breast_overall <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = breast)
km_melanoma <- survfit(
  Surv(time, status) ~ treatment + strata(age),
  data = melanoma
)

iud_last <- max(iud$time)
iud_before_last <- max(iud$time[iud$time < iud_last])
iud_last_event <- max(iud$time[iud$status == 1 & iud$time < iud_last])
```

## 1. From a clinical question to a time-to-event data set

A survival analysis starts with four decisions: the **time origin**, the
**time scale**, the **event** and the **censoring mechanism**. These decisions
are part of the estimand, not a technical detail, and are the same ingredients
used throughout Lecture 1 (see the censoring and recruitment slides). The help
pages
(`?iud`, `?breast`, `?prostate`, `?melanoma`, `?pulmonary`, and
`?sta310r::myeloma`) give the background of each study.

**1.** For each (or some) of the six data sets, describe:

(a) the time origin
(b) time scale unit
(c) the event of interest
(d) what a censored observation means, for example whether the censoring is
administrative, due to loss to follow-up, or due to a competing event.

Some help pages state the origin explicitly; where they do not, say what you
would assume and why. You may answer in a table.

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 1.**

```{r sol-1-table, echo = FALSE}
solution1 <- tibble::tibble(

    paste0("prostate (", nrow(prostate), " men)"),
    paste0("melanoma (", nrow(melanoma), " patients)")

  `Time origin` = c(
```

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**2.** Look at the `prostate` data set. 

(a) How many events are there and how many observations in total?

(b) Create a survfit object: 

```{r}
(surv_prostate <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = prostate))
```

What is the median survival? Is it possible to estimate from the data? 
Interpret the `0.95LCL` and `0.95UCL`.

(c) What can still be estimated from these data?

(d) What happens to the Kaplan–Meier curve after the last death at 69 months,
and why should the far right-hand tail be interpreted cautiously?

(e) Suppose the men who were censored were censored *because they became too
unwell to attend the clinic*. In which direction would the Kaplan–Meier
estimate be biased? What is the name of this assumption violation?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 2.**

*(The median survival time is defined in Lecture 1, slide 25; reporting
survival at fixed times instead of a median is slide 24; and informative
censoring is slide 11.)*

(a) 

```{r}
n_distinct(prostate$patient)
sum(prostate$status)
```

(b) The median is the smallest time at which the estimated survivor function is
below 0.5. The Kaplan–Meier curve for `prostate` never crosses 0.5 and no median exists in the observed follow-up. The reported
lower 95 % limit of the median is a *bound*:
the data are compatible with a median as early as that, but the upper limit is not estimable.

(c) A sensible answer is to report survival at fixed, clinically meaningful
times (for example at 36 and 60 months = 3 and 5 years), with a confidence interval and the number at risk, rather than forcing a
median:

```{r sol-prostate-fixed}
summary(surv_prostate, c(36, 60))
```

(d) 

```{r}
plot(surv_prostate)
last_death <- prostate |>
  filter(status == 1) |>
  summarise(max(time)) |>
  pluck(1)
last_cens <- prostate |> filter(status == 0) |> summarise(max(time)) |> pluck(1)

prostate |> slice_max(time)
```

The last death is at `r last_death` months;
after that the curve is flat until the last censoring at
`r last_cens` months. Only
`r (broom::tidy(surv_prostate) |> slice_tail(n = 1) |> pull(n.risk))` men are at
risk at the last observed time, so the height of the curve there is determined
by a very small risk set. The far right-hand tail should not be interpreted as
a precise estimate of long-term survival.

It is recommended to always present a **risk table** with the Kaplan–Meier curve, 
so that the reader can see how many patients are at risk at each time point:

```{r}
ggsurvfit(surv_prostate) +
  add_risktable() +
  add_confidence_interval()
```

(e) If men who became too unwell stopped attending, their subsequent deaths
would be missing and the remaining men would look healthier than they really
were. The Kaplan–Meier estimate would then be biased **upwards**. This is
**dependent** or **informative censoring**, and it violates the independent
censoring assumption.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**3.** True or false (no programmiong required)?

(a) A patient censored at 10 months is still in the risk set at 12 months.
(b) If censoring is informative, the Kaplan–Meier estimate is always biased
upwards.
(c) The hazard $h(t)$ is the probability of dying at time $t$.
(d) Administrative censoring at the end of a study is usually independent
censoring, provided the analysis time was specified before the data were
examined.
(e) Left censoring means that the true event time is smaller than the observed
time, and interval censoring means that the event time is known only to lie in
an interval.
(f) Study time is calendar time in the study, while patient time is measured
from each patient's own time origin. Administrative censoring at a fixed
calendar date therefore produces different patient-time censoring times for
patients recruited at different dates.


<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 3.**

*(Statements (b), (d), (e) and (f) revisit Lecture 1 (censoring, fixed vs
random censoring, independent censoring, and study vs patient time);
statement (c) is from Lecture 2 on the hazard.)*

(a) **False.** A patient censored at 10 months contributes to the risk set up to
10 months and is removed immediately after 10 months. She is not at risk at 12
months.

(b) **False.** Informative censoring can bias the estimate in either direction.
If high-risk patients leave, survival is overestimated; if low-risk patients
leave, survival is underestimated.

(c) **False.** The hazard is an instantaneous rate, not a probability. It is
the limiting probability of an event in a short interval divided by the length
of that interval, and it can be greater than 1.

(d) **True**, provided the analysis time was specified in advance and the
censoring is not related to prognosis. Administrative censoring at a
pre-specified calendar date is the usual example of independent censoring.

(e) **True.**

(f) **True.**. *Study time* is calendar time measured from the start of the study;
*patient time* is measured from each patient's own time origin. If a study
closes on a fixed calendar date, a patient recruited late has less patient
time at closure than a patient recruited early. Administrative censoring
therefore gives different patient-time censoring times, even though all
patients are censored on the same calendar date. This is usually independent
censoring if the closing date was pre-specified and the recruitment date is
unrelated to prognosis.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

## 2. The empirical survivor function when there is no censoring

The `pulmonary` data contain the survival times of 11 men with pulmonary
metastasis from osteosarcoma, with no censoring. The empirical survivor
function is simply the proportion of men whose survival time is at least $t$:
$$\hat S(t) = \frac{\text{number with survival time} \ge t}{n}.$$
The estimated curve is a step function, constant between adjacent death times
and decreasing at each death time. This is the "estimation of the survival
function" idea from Lecture 1 (slides 15–18), where, with no censoring,
$\hat S(t)$ is simply the proportion still event-free at $t$.

**4.** Explain why this code is useful (interpret what it does, 
include comments and possibly rewrite it in a more readable way). 
Then run it and look at the resulting table:

```{r empirical-table}
emp_pulm <-
  pulmonary |>
  distinct(time) |>
  arrange(time) |>
  mutate(
    n_at_least = map_int(time, \(t) sum(pulmonary$time >= t)),
    S_hat = n_at_least / nrow(pulmonary)
  )
```

(a) Is `S_hat` equivalemnt to the `survival` column from `summary(survfit(Surv(pulmonary$time) ~ 1))`? If not, why?

(b) Plot $\hat S(t)$ above as a step function with ggplot2 (HINT: `geom_step(direction = "vh")`). 
Compare your figure to `survfit2(Surv(time) ~ 1, pulmonary) |> ggsurvfit()`
Are they the same?

(c) At which times does the curve drop, and by how much? Why is the curve flat
between 15 and 17 months?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 4.**

(a) 

```{r}
emp_pulm
summary(survfit(Surv(time) ~ 1, data = pulmonary))
```

There is a small convention issue at an event time. The empirical definition
\(P(T\ge t)\) gives an estimate of `r fmt(emp_pulm$S_hat[1], 3)` at
`r emp_pulm$time[1]` months, because all `r nrow(pulmonary)` men have a
survival time of at least `r emp_pulm$time[1]` months. 
`survfit()` reports `r fmt(10 / 11, 3)` at `r emp_pulm$time[1]` months, 
because it lets the curve drop at the event time and reports the value *after* 
the drop. Between event times the two conventions agree, and at 12 months both 
give `r fmt(10 / 11, 3)`. 
The important practical point is to say whether a reported 
"survival at 12 months" includes deaths at exactly 12 months or not!


(b) The empirical curve is a step function that drops at the event times, and the `ggsurvfit()` version does the same but it starts from time 0 and it adds one extra segment in the end.
(If you use a microscope, the difference in the convention at the event times might be visible as well.)

```{r sol-empirical-table}
emp_pulm |>
  ggplot(aes(time, S_hat)) +
  geom_step(direction = "vh") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  survfit2(Surv(time) ~ 1, pulmonary) |>
    ggsurvfit() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1))
```

It is important to notice, however, that the similarity above would not translate easily to the case with censoring! 
Consider the `prostate` data set:

```{r}
prostate |>
  filter(status == 1) |> # Why?
  distinct(time) |>
  arrange(time) |>
  mutate(
    n_at_least = map_int(time, \(t) sum(prostate$time >= t)),
    S_hat = n_at_least / nrow(prostate)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, S_hat)) +
  geom_step(direction = "vh") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, prostate) |>
    ggsurvfit() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1))
```


(c) With the empirical convention in the table, the estimate is
`r fmt(emp_pulm$S_hat[1], 3)` at `r emp_pulm$time[1]` months and drops at
`r paste(emp_pulm$time[-1], collapse = ", ")` months; the sizes of those drops
are `r paste(fmt(-diff(emp_pulm$S_hat), 3), collapse = ", ")`. It is flat
between `r emp_pulm$time[4]` and `r emp_pulm$time[5]` months because no one
dies in that interval.


<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**5.** The observed times are 
`r paste(sort(pulmonary$time), collapse = ", ")` months.

Their mean is `r mean(pulmonary$time)` months and their median is `r median(pulmonary$time)` months. 
Why is the median usually preferred for survival data? Does the mean or the median describe the
"typical" patient better here? What happens to the mean if the largest
observation is censored?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 5.**

*(Lecture 1, slides 18 and 25: skewed survival times
and the median survival time.)*

Survival times are usually right-skewed
and the mean is sensitive to a few long survivors; the median is the time by
which half the patients have died and is more robust. Here the mean is
slightly larger than the median, which is consistent with a right tail. If the
largest observation were censored, the mean would not be estimable without an
assumption about the unobserved tail; treating the censored time as a death
would *underestimate* the mean. The median can still be estimated if the curve
reaches 0.5.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**6.** Five men die at 13 months. With the convention that the curve drops at
the event time (the convention used by `survfit()`), the estimated survival is
0.909 just before 13 months and 0.455 at 13 months. If one of the men had been
censored at exactly 13 months instead of dying, should that censored
observation be counted *before* or *after* the deaths at 13 months when the
risk set is formed? What difference would the other convention make to the
estimate? 

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 6.**

*Collett discusses this in Section 2.1.2.*

The censored observation should be counted **after** the
deaths at
`r emp_pulm$time[2]` months: the risk set just before that time includes
everyone still under observation at that time, including the person who is
censored there. The deaths are then removed, and the censored observation is
removed afterwards. If the censoring were counted before the deaths, 
the risk set would be too small and the estimated survival would change. 

Note that the time scale here is in months. If exact dates were available, 
the censoring could be counted before or after the deaths depending on the 
exact times of the events. Then the same convention would instead be used for deaths 
and censoring at the same number of days since time 0.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**7. (Optional.)** When there is no censoring, Greenwood's formula reduces to
the binomial standard error
$$\operatorname{se}\{\hat S(t)\} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat S(t)(1-\hat S(t))}{n}}.$$

(a) Use this formula to compute the standard error of $\hat S(13)$ and compare
it with the `std.err` reported by `survfit`.

(b) Why is the standard error `NaN` at the last death time, where
$\hat S(t)=0$? Does that mean the estimate is known with certainty?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 7 (Optional).**

(a) After `r emp_pulm$time[2]` months,
`r sum(pulmonary$time <= emp_pulm$time[2])` of the `r nrow(pulmonary)` men have
died, so
$\hat S(`r emp_pulm$time[2]`)=`r fmt(5 / 11, 4)`$. The binomial standard error
is

$$
\operatorname{se}\{\hat S(13)\}
= \sqrt{\frac{`r fmt(5 / 11, 4)` \times `r fmt(6 / 11, 4)`}{`r nrow(pulmonary)`}}
= `r fmt(sqrt((5 / 11) * (6 / 11) / nrow(pulmonary)), 4)`.
$$
This is the `std.err` reported by `survfit()` at
`r emp_pulm$time[2]` months.

```{r}
pulsurv <- survfit(Surv(time) ~ 1, data = pulmonary)
summary(pulsurv)
```

**NOTE!** `summary()` reports the standard error of the survival estimate, 
whereas `broom::tidy()` reports it on the log-survival scale.
If you want to compute the standard error of the survival estimate from the
`broom::tidy()` output, you need to multiply the `estimate` by the `std.error`:

```{r}
broom::tidy(pulsurv) |>
  select(time, estimate, std.error) |>
  mutate(se_survival = estimate * std.error)
```

(b) At the last death time there is one person at risk and that person dies, so
$\hat S(t)=0$. Greenwood's sum contains the term
$d/(n(n-d))=1/(1\times 0)=\infty$, and $0\times\infty$ is `NaN`. The estimate
is zero because the only remaining person died, but that does not mean the
survival probability is known with certainty; the sample is small and the tail
is poorly estimated. This is one reason why the last part of a Kaplan–Meier
curve is fragile.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->


## 3. Kaplan–Meier

The `iud` data contain the times, in weeks, to discontinuation of an
intrauterine device because of menstrual bleeding problems, for 18 women. Nine
times are events and nine are censored. This is the data set used in Collett's
Examples 2.3–2.10.

The Kaplan–Meier estimator multiplies the survival factors at each event time
(Lecture 1, slides 19–22):
$$\hat S(t)=\prod_{j:\,t_{(j)}\le t}\left(1-\frac{d_j}{n_j}\right),$$
where $d_j$ is the number of events at the event time $t_{(j)}$ and $n_j$ the
number at risk just before it. Question 9 reproduces this product by hand.


**8.** 

(a) Reproduce Collett's Table 2.2. At each event time $t_j$, compute the
number at risk $n_j$, the number of events $d_j$, the survival factor
$(n_j-d_j)/n_j$ and the product-limit estimate.

(b) Report $\hat S(12), \hat S(24), \hat S(52), \hat S(104)$ and $\hat S(107)$.

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 8.**

(a)

```{r sol-km-iud-table}
(t2.2 <- tibble(event_times = sort(unique(iud$time[iud$status == 1]))) |>
  mutate(
    n_risk = map_int(event_times, \(t) sum(iud$time >= t)),
    n_event = map_int(event_times, \(t) sum(iud$time == t & iud$status == 1)),
    factor = (n_risk - n_event) / n_risk,
    estimate = cumprod(factor)
  ))
```

The values agree with Collett's Table 2.2 (exept the first line where no event occured). 

(b) The requested estimates are:

Only the last requested time point is presented in the table:
```{r}
requested_times <- c(12, 24, 52, 104, 107)
t2.2 |>
  filter(event_times %in% requested_times) |>
  select(event_times, estimate)
```

For the remaining ones, we need to look at the closest event time before the requested time point.
For example, for 24 weeks, the closest event time is 19 weeks and the estimte does not change until week 30.

We can also use the `summary()` function to get the estimates from a survfit object:
```{r sol-iud-at-times}
survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = iud) |>
  summary(requested_times)
```
Note that `n.risk` is updated to reflect the number of women at risk at the requested time points (but this does not affect the survival estimate).

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**9.**

(a) The largest observed time (`max(iud$time)`) is 107 weeks, but there is one event and two
censorings at that time. Is $\hat S(t)$ defined for $t>107$? What does the
`survfit` object report?
(b) What would the estimate be beyond 107 if all three observations at 107 had
been censored? What if the only observation at 107 had been an event?
(c) Why does the curve stop at the largest observed time rather than continue
to, say, 120 weeks?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 9.**

(a) The largest observed time is for:

```{r}
slice_max(iud, time)
```
The Kaplan–Meier estimate stays constant from week 97, until just before week 107. 
It is **not defined after 107 weeks**, because there is no one left at risk after
the event and the censorings at week 107.

(b) If all observations at week 107 had been
censored, there would be no event, so the estimate would remain from week 97, 
and it would still be undefined after week 107.
If the only observation at
week 107 had been an event with no other person at risk at that time, the
factor would be $(1-1)/1=0$ and the curve would drop to zero at week 107.

(c) Beyond the largest observed time there is no information about the event
rate; no one is under observation. Continuing the curve flat would assume that
no events occur after the end of follow-up, which is an extra assumption, not a
result of the data. The curve therefore stops at the last observed time.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**10.** The Kaplan–Meier-type hazard estimate in the
interval from $t_{(j)}$ to $t_{(j+1)}$ is
 $$\hat h(t)=\frac{d_j}{n_j\tau_j},\qquad \tau_j=t_{(j+1)}-t_{(j)}.$$
The estimate is not defined after the final death time, because the last interval is
open-ended.

(a) Compute $\hat h(t)$ for the event times in the `iud` data by:

```{r}
event_times <- sort(unique(iud$time[iud$status == 1]))
(haz <- tibble::tibble(
  t = event_times,
  tau = c(diff(event_times), NA_real_),
  n = map_int(event_times, \(t) sum(iud$time >= t)),
  d = map_int(event_times, \(t) sum(iud$time == t & iud$status == 1)),
  h = d / (n * tau)
))
```

Make sure you understand the formula and the code. 
Then interpret the results (you may use a graph).
Why is the ungrouped estimate so much more irregular than a cumulative summary
such as the survivor function?

(b) Why is it usually better to report the cumulative hazard or the survivor
function than a series of raw hazard estimates?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 10.**

(a) 

```{r}
ggplot(haz, aes(t, h)) + geom_step()
```

A similar graph may be produced using the muhaz package, but its kphaz.fit() function uses the event and risk set at the end of each interval and places the estimate at the midpoint.
Hence, the results are slightly different from the above, but the overall shape is similar.

```{r}
library(muhaz)
haz2 <- with(iud, kphaz.fit(time, status, method = "product-limit"))
kphaz.plot(haz2)
```

A single death among a small risk set over a short interval produces a large
and unstable rate; a single death among a large risk set over a long interval
produces a small one.

(b) The cumulative hazard and the survivor function are cumulative summaries:
they use all the information up to time $t$ and are much more stable than a
sequence of pointwise hazard estimates. A raw hazard plot is useful for
exploring shape, but it is not a precise summary, especially in small samples.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**11.** A colleague ignores censoring and estimates 2-year survival in the
`iud` data as "the proportion of women who did not discontinue within 104
weeks".

(a) Compare this with the Kaplan–Meier estimate $\hat S(104)$.
(b) In which direction is the naive estimate biased, and why?
(c) Would the problem be worse or less serious in a study with 80 % censoring?
(d) Write one sentence interpreting $\hat S(104)$ correctly.

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 11.**

(a) 

The naive estimate:

```{r}
naive_events <- filter(iud, status == 1 & time <= 104) |> nrow()
1 - naive_events / nrow(iud)
```

Kaplan–Meier estimate:

```{r}
survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = iud) |>
  summary(104) |>
  _$surv
```

The naive estimate is too high by about 13 percentage points.

(b) The naive calculation treats the `r sum(iud$status == 0)` censored women
as if they had not discontinued during the full `r iud_before_last` weeks. In fact, they were
only followed until their censoring time, and some of them would have
discontinued later. Ignoring that incomplete follow-up inflates the estimated
survival. 

(c) The problem would be worse with 80 % censoring: more of the denominator
would consist of women with incomplete follow-up treated as if they had
completed the study. The bias would generally be larger.

(d) "The estimated probability that a woman is still using the IUD at 104
weeks (2 years) is 0.37, assuming that censoring is non-informative."
Or: "About 37 % of women are estimated to remain free of
discontinuation due to bleeding at 2 years."

<!-- SOLUTION END -->


## 4. Hazard and cumulative hazard

**12.** The cumulative hazard is $H(t)=-\log S(t)$, and the Nelson–Aalen
estimate is the cumulative sum of the event fractions $d_j/n_j$. 

(a) Compare the estimated survival by Kaplan-Meier and Nelson-Aalen for the `sta310r::myeloma` data. 
(HINT: use argument `stype`, see `?survfit.formula()`)?  

Note that `sta310r::myeloma` and `survival::myeloma` are two different data sets 
so use the ::-notation to access the correct version!

(a) How does the estimated survival differ comparing Kaplan–Meier and Nelson–Aalen 
(b) What does the slope of the cumulative hazard curve represent?
(c) The two estimates of $S(t)$ differ by only a few percentage points. Is the
difference practically important compared with the width of the confidence
intervals?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 12.**

*(This is Lecture 2 material: the hazard $h(t)$ is the instantaneous event
rate at time $t$ — the probability of an event in a short interval given no
event before $t$, divided by the interval length — and the cumulative hazard
$H(t)=\int_0^t h(u)\,du$ sums it up.)*

(a)

```{r sol-cumulative-hazard}
# Kaplan–Meier
km <- survfit(
  Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
  data = sta310r::myeloma,
  stype = 1, # "direct" = "Kaplan-Meier" = "product-limit"
  ctype = 1
)

# exp(-Nelson–Aalen)
na_surv <- survfit(
  Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
  data = sta310r::myeloma,
  stype = 2, # exp(cumulative hazard) where cumhaz = Nelson–Aalen from ctype = 1
  ctype = 1
)

bind_rows(km = broom::tidy(km), na = broom::tidy(na_surv), .id = "estimator") |>
  ggplot(aes(time, estimate, color = estimator)) +
  geom_step(direction = "hv")
```

The Nelson–Aalen survivor estimate is larger than the Kaplan–Meier estimate!

(b) The slope of the cumulative hazard curve is the hazard: a steeper slope
means a higher event rate.

```{r}
ggsurvfit(km, type = "cumhaz") +
  ggsurvfit(na_surv, type = "cumhaz")
```

(c) The differences at month 24 in cumulative hazard and survival are
```{r}
summary(na_surv, 24)$cumhaz - summary(km, 24)$cumhaz
summary(na_surv, 24)$surv - summary(km, 24)$surv
```

This is small compared to the SEs:
```{r}
summary(km, 24)$std.err
summary(na_surv, 24)$std.err
```

The difference between the estimators is therefore not practically important compared with the statistical uncertainty.

```{r}
ggsurvfit(km, title = "hej") +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  ggsurvfit(na_surv) +
  add_confidence_interval()
```

<!-- SOLUTION END -->


## 5. Comparing two groups

The `breast` data contain the survival times of 45 women with breast cancer,
classified by whether the tumour stained positively or negatively with the
lectin HPA. There are 13 women in the negative group (5 deaths) and 32 in the
positive group (21 deaths). Collett uses these data in Examples 2.11–2.14.

**13.** 

(a) Plot the Kaplan–Meier curves by staining group, with a risk table and
a line at the median (HINT: look at the example: https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/ggsurvfit/index.html). 

(b) Report $\hat S(24)$, $\hat S(60)$ and $\hat S(120)$ (You may use `gtsummary::tbl_survival()`). 
(c) Interpret the curves in clinical language.
(d) Is the median estimable in both groups? If not, what should be reported
instead?
(e) Do the estimated curves cross? What does the answer suggest about the
relative suitability of the log-rank, Wilcoxon and Peto–Peto tests? *(Collett,
Section 2.6.5; Lecture 2, the log-rank test and the Wilcoxon test)*
(f) Perform a log-rank test to compare the two groups. Report the test statistic and p-value.

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 13.**

(a)

```{r km-breast}
survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ stain, data = breast) |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_quantile(y_value = 0.5) +
  add_risktable() +
  add_pvalue() # vNot asked for but useful to add
```

(b)

```{r tbl-breast}
km_breast <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ stain, data = breast)

tbl_survfit(
  km_breast,
  times = c(24, 60, 120),
  label_header = "**Time {time} months**"
)

summary(km_breast, times = c(24, 60, 120), extend = TRUE)
```

(c) Women with HPA-negative tumours have better survival at every time point.
The direction is consistent with the biological
hypothesis that positive staining marks a tumour with metastatic potential,
but the study is small and observational.

(d) The median is not estimable in the negative group, although its lower 95 % limit is.

```{r}
km_breast
```

(e) The estimated curves do not cross: the negative group is above the
positive group throughout. This is the pattern in which the log-rank test is
the natural default (Collett, Section 2.6.5). The Wilcoxon and Peto–Peto tests
are alternatives that put more weight on early differences; they are more
useful when the curves cross or when the early difference is the hypothesis of
interest.

(f)

The log-rank p-value was already added to the figure above. Alternatively:

```{r}
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ stain, breast, rho = 0) # log-rank
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ stain, breast, rho = 1) # Peto & Peto
```

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

## 6. Three or more groups

The `melanoma` data contain survival times of 30 patients from two
immunotherapy groups, classified into three age groups. *Collett uses the data
in Examples 2.15 and 2.16.* 

**14.** Using only the BCG treatment group, compare survival across the three
age groups with a log-rank test.

(a) What is the null hypothesis? How many degrees of freedom does the test
have?
(b) Report the test statistic and p-value. Which age group contributes most to
the test statistic?
(c) Interpret the test results

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 14.**

```{r}
bcg <- melanoma |> filter(treatment == 1)
```
(a) The null hypothesis is that the survival distributions are the same in the
three age groups among patients treated with BCG.
There are `r n_distinct(bcg$age)` groups, so the test has
`r n_distinct(bcg$age) - 1` degrees of freedom.



```{r melanoma-three-groups}
(x <- survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ age, data = bcg))
```


(b) The test statistic is `r x$chisq`, p = `r x$pvalue`.
The oldest group (age = 3) contributes most (biggest difference between observed and expected).

(c) 

```{r}
table(bcg$age)
```

The three age groups are small, so the test has very little power. 
A non-significant result is not evidence that the groups are
the same; it means that these data are compatible with no difference. The
small numbers also make the asymptotic chi-square approximation questionable.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**15.** Now compare the two treatments (`treatment` variable), first without and then with
stratification by age group (HINT: `strata(age)` in the formula).

(a) Report the test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value for both tests.
(b) What does the stratified test estimate that the unstratified test does
not? What assumption does the stratified test make about the treatment effect
across age groups?
(c) Why are the two results so similar here? Check the distribution of age
group within each treatment group.
(d) Give an example of a situation in which stratification would change the
conclusion.

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 15.**

(a)

```{r melanoma-stratified}
bind_rows(
  unstratified = survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ treatment, melanoma) |>
    broom::glance(),
  stratified = survdiff(
    Surv(time, status) ~ treatment + strata(age),
    data = melanoma
  ) |>
    broom::glance(),
  .id = "analysis"
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

(b) The stratified test compares the treatments *within* each age stratum and
combines the observed-minus-expected differences and their variances across
strata. It estimates a common treatment effect while allowing each age group
to have its own baseline hazard. It assumes that the treatment effect is the
same in each age stratum (no treatment-by-age interaction) and that the
strata are comparable in the sense required by the test.

(c) The age distribution is fairly balanced between the treatment groups:

```{r sol-melanoma-age-table}
gtsummary::tbl_summary(melanoma, treatment, include = age) |>
  gtsummary::add_difference(~"smd")
```

Age does not appear to be a strong confounder here. Stratification removes a
small amount of age imbalance but does not change the conclusion.

(d) Stratification can change the conclusion when age (or another stratifying
factor) is strongly prognostic and the treatment groups differ substantially
in its distribution. For example, if older patients were much more likely to
receive one treatment and older age strongly increased mortality, the
unstratified test could attribute the age effect to treatment. A stratified
test would remove that confounding. If the treatment effect itself differs
across strata, a common-effect stratified test may be misleading, and
stratum-specific estimates or an interaction test would be needed.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->
